introduction-serverless-containers.core: Fargate runs containers without servers: you specify CPU and memory per task or pod, and AWS provisions an isolated Firecracker microVM for it. No AMIs, patching, cluster capacity or bin packing. You pay per vCPU-second and GB-second, and it works with both ECS and EKS.

first_principles.problem: A team spends time patching and scaling EC2 hosts for a handful of container services.
truths: Some flexibility is lost (no host access).
derivation: Accept limits: **no privileged/host mode, no DaemonSets on EKS**.

analogy.title: Taking taxis instead of owning a car
analogy.story: No maintenance or parking, and you pay per trip, but you can't modify the engine.
analogy.breaks: Taxis are shared; each Fargate task gets its own isolated microVM.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Container runs with no servers to manage.

code.text:
aws ecs run-task --cluster prod --launch-type FARGATE --task-definition report:12 \
  --network-configuration 'awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-a],securityGroups=[sg-1],assignPublicIp=DISABLED}'

check.q: What isolation boundary does each Fargate task get?
check.a: Its own Firecracker microVM, not shared with other tasks.

fargate-platform-versions-13-vs-14.core: Fargate platform versions define the runtime environment. Platform 1.4.0 (current Linux baseline) moved to containerd, routes all task traffic (including image pulls and secrets) through the task ENI, added 20 GB+ ephemeral storage (configurable to 200 GB), EFS support and better metrics. 1.3.0 used a separate Fargate-owned ENI for platform traffic.

first_principles.problem: After moving to 1.4.0, tasks in private subnets fail to pull images because they lack a route or VPC endpoints.
truths: Platform traffic now uses your ENI.
Network paths must allow ECR, S3 and Secrets Manager.
derivation: Provide **NAT or VPC endpoints** (ecr.api, ecr.dkr, s3, logs, secretsmanager).

analogy.title: A building where deliveries now use your front door
analogy.story: Previously the landlord had a separate service entrance; now everything comes through your door, so it must be open.
analogy.breaks: Delivery doors don't need routing tables; ENIs do.

example.title: Private subnet requirements
flow: Interface endpoints: ecr.api, ecr.dkr, logs, secretsmanager

check.q: Why might Fargate 1.4.0 tasks fail to pull images in private subnets?
check.a: Image pulls go through the task ENI, so the subnet needs NAT or VPC endpoints for ECR and S3.

fargate-networking-the-eni-per-task-mode.core: Every Fargate task (or EKS Fargate pod) gets its own ENI with a private IP in your subnet, using awsvpc mode. Each task can have its own security groups and appears in flow logs, but tasks consume subnet IPs and ENI quotas, and ENI attachment adds a few seconds to startup.

first_principles.problem: A burst of 2,000 tasks fails because the subnets run out of IP addresses.
truths: One ENI per task means one IP per task.
derivation: Keep tasks **private**; use ALB for ingress.

analogy.title: Each tenant gets their own front door and doorbell
analogy.story: Great for security and identity, but you need enough doors.
analogy.breaks: Buildings plan doors at construction; subnet size is likewise fixed later.

check.q: What resource does each Fargate task consume in your subnet?
check.a: One ENI with one private IP address.

fargate-pricing-the-math-that-matters.core: Fargate bills per second for requested vCPU and memory (plus extra ephemeral storage), from start to stop, rounded up to one minute minimum. It costs more per unit than well-packed EC2, but you pay nothing for idle host capacity. Fargate Spot (up to ~70% off), Graviton (ARM, ~20% cheaper) and Compute Savings Plans cut the cost.

first_principles.problem: A team compares Fargate's per-vCPU price to EC2 and concludes it's too expensive, ignoring EC2 idle capacity and ops time.
truths: EC2 clusters rarely run at 100% utilisation.
Fargate charges only for task size.

analogy.title: A hotel room versus renting a whole flat
analogy.story: Per night, the hotel costs more, but you don't pay for empty rooms.
analogy.breaks: Hotels have fixed room sizes; Fargate sizes are flexible within valid combinations.

check.q: Why can Fargate be cheaper overall despite higher unit prices?
check.a: You don't pay for idle host capacity or the engineering time to manage and pack EC2 hosts.
